Cover the pan with a lid and turn off the cooker.
And keep paper and towels away from the cooker.
One more rule: always clean up after yourself.
A clean kitchen is a safe kitchen.
At the end of the lesson nobody was hurt, and the vegetable soup was excellent.

Each friend agreed to bring something.
Sasha made sandwiches with cheese, ham and cucumber.
She cut them into triangles because they look nicer that way.
Maksym brought a big bottle of lemonade.
He made it himself with lemons, mint and honey.
It was a bit too sour, but nobody complained.

It was still a little warm when she brought it.
He brought apples, grapes and a watermelon, but he forgot a knife!

Diana brought the blanket, paper plates and a bag for rubbish.
We must leave the park clean,
They ate, played badminton, laughed and took lots of photos.

You don't need a knife for bananas!
Every region of Ukraine has its own special dishes.
If you travel around the country, your stomach will be very happy!
Borshch is the most famous Ukrainian dish.
There are dozens of recipes, and every family thinks theirs is the best.
In Poltava they add small dumplings called halushky.
In the west some families make a clear red borshch for Christmas Eve.
People fill them with potatoes, cabbage, cheese or cherries.
In summer cherry varenyky with sour cream are a real treat.
In the Carpathians you must try banosh.
People make it from cornmeal and sour cream and cook it over a fire.
People serve it with mushrooms and brynza, a salty sheep's cheese.
In Crimea the Crimean Tatars cook chebureky and yantyky, crispy pies with meat.
Try Kyiv cake, with nuts, meringue and cream.
People bring it as a present when they visit friends.
Ukrainian food is simple, filling and made with love.
Eat, eat, you are too thin!
Our class newspaper has a food column.
This month Maryna, 13, visited a new café called "Honey Bear" and wrote a review.
"Honey Bear opened in our town last month, and there is always a queue.
I went there with my parents on Saturday to find out why.
The café is small and cosy, with wooden tables and plants everywhere.
On the walls there are photos of bees and old honey jars.
It smells of fresh bread and cinnamon.
The menu is not very long, but everything sounds delicious.
I ordered pancakes with honey and berries, and a hot chocolate.
My dad chose a mushroom omelette, and my mum had a vegetable soup with fresh bread.
The pancakes were soft and warm, and the berries were fresh.
The hot chocolate was a bit too sweet for me, but my dad loved it.
The soup was the best part of the meal, my mum says.
The waiters were friendly and fast, even though the café was full.
Prices are fair: a meal for three cost about the same as a pizza.
Next time I want to try the honey cake!"
Our biology teacher asked us to keep a food diary for one week.
It's Thursday evening, and this is what I have written so far.
This week I have eaten a lot of fruit.
I have had an apple every day, and yesterday I tried a mango for the first time.
I have drunk more water than usual.
Our teacher says we need about six glasses a day.
I haven't reached six yet, but I've drunk four or five every day.
I have already eaten fish twice: salmon on Monday and fish soup today.
I have never liked fish much, but Mum's fish soup is changing my mind.
Unfortunately, I have also eaten too many sweets.

I've had three pieces this week!

Christmas is one of the most important holidays in many countries.
It celebrates the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem more than two thousand years ago.
But every nation has its own way to celebrate it.
In Ukraine Christmas Eve is a family evening.
People wait for the first star in the sky, and then the family sits down to a supper of twelve dishes.
The most important dish is kutia, made of wheat, honey, poppy seeds and nuts.
The day after, children go carolling.
They sing old songs called koliadky and receive sweets and money.
Many Ukrainian traditions have a link to the land and to the year of a farmer.
The didukh, a sheaf of wheat in the corner of the room, represents the spirits of the family and a good harvest.
Some families go to a midnight mass.
Others decorate their homes with embroidered towels with old patterns.
Every region has its own pattern, and some families believe that each pattern belongs to their own family.
What do all these traditions have in common?
Even people who are not religious relate to these traditions, because they connect us with our grandparents.
Our class made a calendar of holidays for the classroom wall.
Each student chose one month and wrote about a holiday.
January: Christmas and New Year are over, but on the 22nd of January we celebrate the Day of Unity of Ukraine.
February: On the 14th of February people give cards and flowers to people they love.
March: On the 8th of March many people give flowers to their mothers, grandmothers and teachers.
April or May: Easter is a moving holiday, so the date changes every year.
We paint pysanky and take Easter baskets to church.
June: On the 1st of June we celebrate Children's Day.
Many towns have concerts and games in the parks.
August: On the 24th of August we celebrate Independence Day.
People wear embroidered shirts, called vyshyvankas, and people decorate the cities with blue and yellow flags.
December: On the 6th of December we have St Nicholas Day.
Children find small presents under their pillows in the morning, but only if they were good!
Most students said St Nicholas Day.
Presents under the pillow are hard to beat!
At midnight on the 31st of December, people all over the world welcome the New Year.
But the traditions are very different.
In Spain people eat twelve grapes at midnight, one grape for each stroke of the clock.
Each grape represents a lucky month.
In Denmark people smash old plates on the doors of their friends' houses.
According to tradition, the more broken plates you find in the morning, the more friends you have.
In Colombia some people walk around the block with an empty suitcase.
They hope that the new year will bring lots of travel.
In Scotland the first person who enters your house after midnight is very important.
A tall, dark-haired man with a piece of coal brings good luck.
In Japan bells in Buddhist temples ring 108 times to clean away the bad things of the old year.
In Ukraine families decorate a New Year tree, cook a big dinner and watch fireworks.
At midnight everybody makes a wish.
Pysanky are decorated Easter eggs, and they are one of the most famous symbols of Ukraine.
They are made with wax and natural dyes, and every pattern has a meaning.
First, a raw egg is washed and dried.
Then a pattern is drawn on the egg with hot wax.
A special tool called a kistka is used for this.
Next, the egg is put into a light dye, usually yellow.
The parts with wax stay white.
Then more wax is added, and the egg is put into a darker dye, for example red.
At the end the wax is melted near a candle and removed.
In the past, pysanky were made only by women, often at night when the children were asleep.
Each pattern was kept in the family and passed from mother to daughter.
A sun means life, a wave means water, and wheat means a good harvest.
Today pysanky are collected all over the world.
There is even a giant pysanka in Kolomyia.
It is a museum, and it is visited by thousands of people every year.
Christmas in Britain is celebrated on the 25th of December.
Houses are decorated with lights, and evergreen plants, like holly and ivy, are hung over doors and fireplaces.
The Christmas tree is covered with shiny balls and lights.
On Christmas Eve children hang stockings by the fireplace.
They believe that Father Christmas comes down the chimney at night and fills the stockings with presents.
Children usually leave a mince pie and a carrot for him and his reindeer.
On Christmas Day the family has a big dinner with roast turkey, potatoes and vegetables.
Before the meal everybody pulls a cracker.
It's a paper tube which makes a loud bang.
Inside there is a paper crown, a small toy and a joke.
In Scotland, New Year is even more important than Christmas.
At the last stroke of midnight people hold hands and sing "Auld Lang Syne", an old song about friendship written by the poet Robert Burns.
Many families also provide food and presents for people who are alone or poor at Christmas.
For many British people, that is the real spirit of Christmas.
On the last Friday before the winter holidays our English club had a Christmas quiz night.
The quizmaster was our teacher, Ms Koval, in a red hat.
Christmas in Ukraine is on the 25th of December, isn't it?
"Father Christmas doesn't come down the chimney in Ukraine, does he?"
St Nicholas puts presents under our pillows!"
Some students said yes, some said no.
Then teams answered harder questions about Christmas in other countries.
Team Snowflakes knew that people in Australia often celebrate Christmas on the beach, because it's summer there.
Team Reindeer knew that in Norway people hide their brooms on Christmas Eve, so witches can't steal them.
The last question was a crossword.
The teams had to find ten Christmas words: star, carol, candle, gift, angel, snow, tree, bell, wish and kutia.
In the end Team Reindeer won by one point.
Their prize was a big box of gingerbread biscuits, which they shared with everybody.
That was a nice ending, wasn't it?
Not all holidays are about winter.
In the USA one of the most important holidays is Thanksgiving, on the fourth Thursday of November.
Its history goes back four centuries.
In 1620 a group of English settlers sailed to America on a ship called the Mayflower.
The journey was dreadful: it lasted more than two months, and many people were ill.
Their first winter was very hard, and half of them died.
The local Native Americans showed the settlers how to grow corn and where to catch fish.
In autumn 1621, after a good harvest, the settlers and the Native Americans had a big meal together.
This is remembered as the first Thanksgiving.
Today families get together and eat roast turkey with gravy, cranberry sauce and pumpkin pie.
Before the meal many families say a blessing or tell each other what they are thankful for.
In Ukraine we have a different tradition of giving thanks for food: Lent.
Before Easter many people give up meat, milk or sweets for some weeks.
When Easter comes, the first meal tastes like the best meal of the year.
Both traditions teach the same thing: be thankful for what you have.
